title: The merge is the payoff
hook: Splitting cards into piles looks like extra work. It isn't.
misconception: Splitting a problem into pieces adds work; merging is cleanup at the end.
objective: The learner can explain why merging two sorted piles of total size n needs at most n-1 comparisons, and why that makes splitting worthwhile.

claims.text: Merging two sorted lists with n elements in total takes at most n-1 comparisons.
claims.source: Each comparison outputs one element; the last element needs no comparison. Knuth, TAOCP Vol. 3, 5.2.4.

claims.text: Merge Sort sorts 1,000 items in fewer than 10,000 comparisons in the worst case.
claims.source: Worst case n*ceil(log2 n) - 2^ceil(log2 n) + 1 = 1000*10 - 1024 + 1 = 8,977 (Knuth, TAOCP Vol. 3, 5.2.4).

claims.text: Comparing every one of 1,000 cards with every other takes 499,500 comparisons.

recall.question: Two sorted piles hold 10 cards in total. What is the most comparisons a merge needs?
recall.why: Every comparison places one card for good, and the last card needs none.
